fields.connection: V (plain form) / N + としたところで
examples: Even if the budget were increased, the deadline would not change.
Even if he apologized, the victims' anger would probably not subside.
Even for children, that footage is shocking.
Even a genius cannot achieve results without effort.
Even if we started over now, there is no guarantee we would make it in time.
Even I have absolutely no intention of defending him.
fields.explain:
Used to acknowledge a possibility while asserting that the conclusion does not change (limited/ineffective).
The style is somewhat more formal/academic than 〜たところで and 〜としても.
The second clause usually avoids commands/strong volition; it focuses on objective evaluation.

• Meaning: strong hypothetical concession, “even if/suppose that … (still) … the result does not change (usually negative/limited)”.
• Mild nuance of criticism/pessimism, emphasizing futility or the difficulty of changing the situation.
• Goes with negative and limiting expressions: 〜ない／たいした〜ない／所詮〜／わけではない often appear in the second clause.
• にしたところで emphasizes “even for (that person/group)”. としたところで is more neutral and applies to clauses.
fields.notes:
• Add たとえ／仮に to emphasize a supposition far from reality.
• In argumentation, this pattern helps “block” a counterargument: it acknowledges the other side's point but preserves the conclusion.
• Should not be used with a direct desire (〜たい) in the second clause; keep the nuance of evaluation/judgment.
mistakes: Confusing it with 〜とすると (inferential condition). 〜としたところで is a concession; the result is usually negative/limited.
Lacking a negative nuance in the second clause → the sentence sounds forced. Use 〜ない／限らない／たいした〜ない…
Changing “にしたところで” to “をしたところで” with a noun → wrong particle. It must be に.
Trap: choosing between 〜としても and 〜としたところで. If the style is formal and the result is strongly negative → prefer 〜としたところで.

rows: Formal; applies to clauses or N
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>だとしたところで…
Even if (to the point of having done it)
Attaches directly to V-た; more colloquial
<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるとしても<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>びはある
にしたって is colloquial; close in meaning to にしたところで

examples: If it rains, the match will be canceled.
If the company president is coming, we have to make thorough preparations.
If a life is at stake, this is no time to hesitate.
If he is in charge, we can rest easy.
If we are expanding overseas, checking legal regulations is essential.
fields.explain:
Used when: stating a major/important condition and then drawing a principled conclusion.
Often appears in written language, reports, and presentations of opinions/policy.
The second clause feels like “something inevitable/something that should be done” rather than a light personal suggestion.
Combines well with emphatic words: いざ、いよいよ、本当に、万一.

• Main meaning: “If (in the case that) A, then B is natural/inevitable/worth doing”.
• Nuance: reasoned, general; used to state principles, general tendencies, or a firm decision when the condition is significant enough.
• Compared with となると: less about “discussing a specific matter”, leaning toward general judgments/opinions. Compared with となったら: more formal and less personal.
• The second clause is often a firm conclusion/strong opinion: ～に違いない、～は避けられない、～べきだ、～ことになる.
fields.notes:
• Often used to state a “standard of action”: A となれば B すべきだ/不可避だ/当然だ.
• Suitable for opening a paragraph in argumentative writing: “X となれば、Y は避けられないだろう”。
• The tone is more formal than となると; avoid using it for momentary emotions unless emphasizing “いざ”.
• Often combined with abstract nouns: 例外、危機、非常事態、国家レベル、法的問題.
mistakes: Using となれば in light everyday conversation can sound stiff; consider となると/となったら.
A weak desire (～たい/～ませんか) in the second clause is less natural; replace it with a judgment/obligation.
JLPT: When the question calls for a nuance of “principle/inevitability/broad supposition”, choose となれば; when it calls for “a specific problem arising”, choose となると.

rows: General, formal, strong sense of inevitability
<ruby>非常<rt>ひじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>事態<rt>じたい</rt></ruby>となれば、<ruby>避難<rt>ひなん</rt></ruby>だ。
If it comes to/speaking of A, then...
<ruby>海外<rt>かいがい</rt></ruby><ruby>勤務<rt>きんむ</rt></ruby>となると、<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>がかかる。
If/when the time comes for A, then...
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すとなったら、<ruby>片<rt>かた</rt></ruby>づけよう。
やる<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>全力<rt>ぜんりょく</rt></ruby>で。

examples: The children must have been tired; they are sound asleep on the train home.
The sky has suddenly grown dark. It looks like it is going to rain, and the wind has picked up too.
He seems to be worried about something; he has been down for the past few days.
The new product seems to be popular; stock has been low since the first day of sale.
They seem to have stayed up all night; there are dark circles under their eyes.
She seems to be in no hurry to reply; the message is still just marked as read.
fields.explain:
Framework: A is evidence → the speaker infers B (a judgment). Not used when there is no concrete sign.
Objective nuance: the speaker steps back slightly to observe, avoiding a sense of imposing a subjective view.
Often accompanied by words indicating signs: 見たところ／様子から／どうやら／最近～／数字を見ると… → increases reliability.
Restriction: usually does not combine with a direct command/volition in clause B.
Written style: in news/reports, the sentence-final form ～とみえる may be used.

～とみえて expresses a judgment, “ it seems that…/apparently…”, based on observable signs (behavior, state, a specific situation). The speaker does not assert absolutely but infers from the facts at hand.

•
Objectivity: there is visible evidence (facial expressions, weather, crowds, figures…).

•
Position: usually in the middle of the sentence: Clause A (observed basis) ＋ とみえて ＋ Clause B (judgment).

•
Degree of certainty: higher than ～ようだ/～みたいだ when A is “strong evidence”. Lower than 断定.

•
Style: often used in written language, reports, and commentary; also natural in formal conversation.
fields.notes:
•
Implicit inference chart:
Sign A → Hypothesis H → Soft judgment B. ～とみえて sits between observation and conclusion, helping the sentence “stay soft”.
•
Suitable for academic/journalistic style: used to describe social phenomena or market tendencies when there are no conclusive figures yet.
•
Reliability: increases when A is figures, weather, or repeated behavior; decreases when A is only a passing feeling.
•
Shifting to a polite tone: in clause B, use ～ようです／～でしょう to increase objectivity.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～らしい:
～らしい is based on an information source; ～とみえて is based on observation. Exam questions often set traps around the source of information.
Confusing it with ～ようだ／～みたいだ: when the question has “concrete evidence” (figures, a clear phenomenon), prefer ～とみえて.
Omitting 「だ」 with nouns/na-adjectives: N/Aな＋ だ＋とみえて → in spoken language it is sometimes omitted, but exam questions usually require the standard form.
Using it with a command/volition: unnatural. Avoid sentences like「遅れるとみえて、急ぎなさい」。Separate the judgment and the command.
Missing the observation clause A:
～とみえて needs A as its basis. If there is no sign, use a different pattern.
Getting the direction of cause and effect wrong: A is the sign and B is the judgment, not an explanation of a definite reason.

rows: A judgment based on observable signs.
Emphasizes “concrete evidence”. Usually in the middle of the sentence.
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い とみえて、<ruby>入口<rt>いりぐち</rt></ruby>で<ruby>混雑<rt>こんざつ</rt></ruby>している。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい とみえる。
Less emphasis on concrete evidence; more colloquial (～みたいだ).
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る みたいだ。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>中<rt>ちゅう</rt></ruby>らしい。
Emphasizes outward appearance, without deep inference.
<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>がない ように<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える。

fields.meaning: For someone in the position of… to…
examples: To think that a doctor, of all people, would downplay the dangers of smoking.
It is hard to believe that a teacher, of all people, would verbally abuse students.
Someone who is a national leader should not keep making baseless statements.
Tampering with data is unacceptable for someone in the position of a researcher.
To think that the president of a leading company, of all people, would be late for a meeting.
fields.explain:
The agent is usually a noun carrying prestige: 医者,教師,研究者,社長,公務員, プロ,一流企業など.
The second clause usually contains a negative evaluation or unmet expectations; it is rarely used for praise.
Combines naturally with the topic particle/subject particle: ～が／は; followed by ～とは/～なんて to emphasize exclamation.
Avoid using it about yourself unless you intend strong self-criticism.
Style: formal, rhetorical; suited to editorials, news, and disciplinary reports.

• Expresses surprise, criticism, or high expectations toward a person/organization with high status, prestige, or expertise who nonetheless does something unbecoming.
• Implies that being “someone like X”, one “should not/cannot” do such a thing, or “ought to have…”.
• Formal nuance, often seen in news, commentary, and written language; also used in spoken language but feels heavy.
• Often followed by a second clause carrying emotion: ～とは、～なんて、～べきだ、～あるまじき.
fields.notes:
• The form ものが after ともあろう strengthens the nuance of criticism: ～ともあろう者が.
• Usually comes before a noun referring to a person; rarely used for things/concepts unless personified (例: 国家ともあろう存在).
• Combine with まさか/まことに to raise the degree of exclamation: まさか医者ともあろう人が…
mistakes: Using it for a target without clear “status” → wrong nuance. Choose a noun with standing.
Using direct praise in the second clause → goes against the typical feeling. It is mainly used for criticism/surprise.
Confusing it with ～たる者: ～ともあろう expresses something blameworthy that “has happened”; ～たる者 states a recommended standard.
Omitting the exclamatory particle (とは/なんて) makes the sentence less natural when you want to emphasize emotion.

rows: <ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>ともあろう<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>がミスを？
Normative; does not necessarily criticize an action that has occurred
<ruby>指導<rt>しどう</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>たる<ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>誠実<rt>せいじつ</rt></ruby>であるべきだ。
<ruby>教師<rt>きょうし</rt></ruby>にあるまじき<ruby>行為<rt>こうい</rt></ruby>。
An N of the caliber of… and yet…
プロほどの<ruby>選手<rt>せんしゅ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>凡<rt>凡</rt></ruby>ミスをするとは。

examples: Once you are a working adult, how you use your time is put to the test.
When the end of the year comes around, every store gets crowded.
Once children reach high school, they tend to stop listening to their parents.
When it comes to the real thing, you sometimes cannot perform as well as usual.
When it comes to working overseas, family support is indispensable.
fields.explain:
First clause: a noun expressing a milestone/status:社会人,管理職,年末,本番,受験シーズン.
Second clause: a new consequence/condition, usually a rule/natural consequence rather than personal volition.
Not used to state a single chance event; suited to describing general tendencies.
Different from ともなれば: ～ともなると sounds more colloquial and has more direct emphasis.

• Once the stage/status/situation X is reached, the situation/standards/needs change significantly.
• Nuance of “whenever/once… then”, with a sense of moving up a level. The second clause usually describes a natural consequence or higher demands.
• Often used in explanations and commentary; natural in both spoken and written language.
fields.notes:
• Often goes with “threshold” milestones: 本番, 期末, 繁忙期, 子育て, 老後.
• Combine with いざ to emphasize the gap between preparation and the real thing: いざ～ともなると…
• Can be used at the beginning of a sentence as an adverbial phrase: 夏休みともなると、…
mistakes: Using it directly with verbs: this pattern prefers a noun as the milestone, not V＋ともなると.
A single personal volition in the second clause → less natural. State a general/inevitable consequence.
Confusing it with となると (topicalization). ～ともなると means “reaching a stage”, not “speaking of”.

rows: <ruby>管理<rt>かんり</rt></ruby><ruby>職<rt>しょく</rt></ruby>ともなると<ruby>責任<rt>せきにん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>年末<rt>ねんまつ</rt></ruby>ともなれば<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。
If speaking of/when it comes to… then…
Topicalization; does not necessarily mean “reaching a stage”
<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>となると<ruby>張<rt>は</rt></ruby>り<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る。
On the occasion of/when carrying out
<ruby>入学<rt>にゅうがく</rt></ruby>にあたっての<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>。

examples: When the end of the fiscal year comes, overtime increases in every department.
Once you become a manager, the responsibility for decision-making grows heavier.
Once you are in the child-rearing years, both expenses and time add up.
For a big city, developing disaster prevention plans is essential.
Should a disaster actually strike, sending out accurate information is the top priority.
fields.explain:
The first clause is a noun as a milestone; the second clause states an inevitable consequence or a normative requirement.
Works well in guidance documents, regulations, and internal notices.
Compared with ～ともなると, it feels more “argumentative” and less colloquial.

• Similar to ～ともなると: once the milestone/status X is reached, certain conditions/standards/consequences follow.
• Sounds formal; often used in official announcements, guidance, and news.
• Often combined with rule-like/procedural content: 必要となる／求められる／増える／避けられない.
fields.notes:
• Combines easily with passive verbs/intransitive stative verbs: 増える・求められる・必要となる.
• Often appears in administrative documents, corporate materials, and political/social news.
• Can open a paragraph to set the context before laying out regulations.
mistakes: Using a direct verb clause in the first clause → unnatural. It must be a noun as the milestone.
A single specific personal action in the second clause → less natural; state a general tendency/consequence.
Confusing the nuance with となると (speaking of): ともなれば means “reaching a stage”, a turning point.

rows: <ruby>年度<rt>ねんど</rt></ruby><ruby>末<rt>まつ</rt></ruby>ともなれば<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby><ruby>物<rt>ぶつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>ともなると<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。
To the point of/reaching the stage of
Emphasizes the “extreme point”; not necessarily a social milestone
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>き、<ruby>撤退<rt>てったい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>っては…
A procedural condition rather than a social milestone
<ruby>申請<rt>しんせい</rt></ruby>する<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>すべき<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>。

fields.connection: V (plain form) + とも + V (plain form) + とも / N + N / A + A
examples: He didn't say whether he would go or not.
This plan cannot be definitively called either a success or a failure.
The economy is in a state that can be called neither good nor bad.
The effectiveness of this medicine cannot be called either high or low.
His expression is hard to read: it could be joy or it could be anger.
This sentence can be taken as either sarcasm or a joke.
fields.explain:
Used when a conclusion has not been or cannot be reached, or when deliberately avoiding commitment; suited to written language, reports, and commentary.
What follows is usually a negative/hard-to-determine expression: ～言えない／決められない／断定できない／わからない／はっきりしない.
With verbs, the common contrast is: VるともVないとも…; with -い adjectives: AいともAくないとも…; with -な adjectives and nouns: だ is usually omitted before とも.
If the focus is on “saying/answering”: ～とも～とも言わない／返事しない → “not say (out loud) A or B”.
The form “～とも～ともつかない／取れる” emphasizes ambiguity/multiple meanings in expressions, texts, and attitudes.
Usually exactly two options are listed; if there are more than two, consider other patterns such as ～やら～やら.

• Presents two possibilities/options A and B and then denies that a decision can be made: “cannot say whether it is A or B”, “cannot yet decide whether it is A or B”.
• Used to describe the speaker/other party “not saying clearly whether A or B”: AともBとも言わない.
• Emphasizes ambiguity and two-way possibility: AともBともつかない／取れる → “can be understood as A or B”, “hard to tell”.
• Formal nuance, leaning toward writing or careful statements; avoids definitive assertions.
• Often accompanied by verbs/expressions: 言えない, 言わない, 決められない, 分からない, 断定できない, 判断がつかない, はっきりしない, つかない, 取れる.
• Often combined with antonym pairs: 賛成/反対, 成功/失敗, 良い/悪い, 高い/安い, 有罪/無罪… to highlight “not leaning to either side”.
fields.notes:
• In terms of form, with -な words and nouns, だ is usually omitted before とも: 便利とも不便とも; 成功とも失敗とも.
• The two parts before とも should be grammatically parallel (same part of speech/same level of negation, or a clear antonym pair) for the sentence to be natural.
• In spoken language, a shortened form is often used: どっちとも言えない instead of listing both in full.
• Do not confuse it with とも meaning “even if” (たとえ～とも); it also differs from 何とも (not… at all) and ～ともなく (unconscious/vague about the agent).
• Often appears in legal documents, research reports, and financial commentary, where cautious language that avoids strong assertions is needed.
mistakes: Using more than 2 options: ～とも～とも is natural only with exactly two possibilities; for more than two, use ～やら～やら or another kind of listing.
Confusing it with ～にせよ／であれ: these two patterns mean “whether A or B” (regardless), not “cannot say whether A or B”.
Attaching a strongly affirmative predicate: ～とも～とも is usually followed by a negative/hard-to-determine expression; avoid attaching a definitive judgment.
Wrong -な form: writing 便利だとも不便だとも… is not absolutely wrong, but だ is usually omitted to sound more natural: 便利とも不便とも…
Not grammatically parallel: 高いとも安くないとも… sounds forced; use a balanced pair: 高いとも安いとも… or 高いとも高くないとも…
Confusing it with AかBか in questions: AかBか asks for a choice; AともBとも言えない is a comment that no conclusion can be drawn.
JLPT reading trap: the phrase ～とも～ともつかない/取れる expresses “ambiguity”; do not translate it as “both A and B” (and) but as “hard to say whether A or B / can be understood either way”.

rows: Cannot/does not say clearly whether A or B; ambiguous
Emphasizes “not deciding”; often goes with <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない・<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わない・つかない・<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>れる
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>不<rt>ふ</rt></ruby><ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
Neutral, no implied ambiguity; used in questions/choices
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないか<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めて
どちらとも<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
Similar content but general; does not list a specific pair
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>はどちらとも<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
～にせよ／にしろ～にせよ／にしろ
Expresses “regardless”, unlike the “not deciding” of ～とも～とも
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>にせよ<ruby>不<rt>ふ</rt></ruby><ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>にせよ<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>する
Whether A or B (it is all the same)
Inclusive reasoning/condition; no nuance of ambiguity
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>歓迎<rt>かんげい</rt></ruby>だ
Gives more than 2 examples; not “cannot conclude A/B”
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>やらノートやらで<ruby>鞄<rt>かばん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い
Describes repetition/contrast; no meaning of “not deciding”
<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れたり<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だったりする
AともBともつかない／<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>れる
Cannot be determined; can be understood in 2 ways
A sub-variant of ～とも～とも, leaning toward “ambiguity of interpretation”
<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>れる
